title: Paris in 1900 had a two-speed moving sidewalk, 7 metres above the street

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still of men in hats standing on a raised moving walkway in 1900, one holding an upright post, with trees and buildings behind a railing.

body: The 1900 Paris Exposition covered 216 hectares, so simply getting around it was a challenge. The **Rue de l’Avenir**, or ‘Street of the Future’, was a moving sidewalk that ran from the esplanade of Les Invalides to the Champ de Mars with nine stations. Passengers climbed to a platform 7 m above the ground, stepped onto a walkway moving at **4.2 km/h**, then across to a faster one at **8.5 km/h**. Posts with handles gave them something to hold, or they could keep walking.

slides.alt: Black-and-white film of visitors in hats and long coats riding a raised moving walkway at the 1900 Paris Exposition, some holding upright posts, past a railing, trees and buildings.
slides.caption: Visitors ride the moving sidewalk at the 1900 Paris Exposition, some gripping its upright posts, in a film by Edison’s company.

slides.heading: How to ride the Street of the Future

steps.label: Climb to a platform 7 m up
Step across to the 8.5 km/h one
Hold a post, or keep walking

slides.heading: Getting around the 1900 fair: higher or lower?
slides.explanation: A Decauville electric train followed the same route at an average of 17 km/h, twice the speed of the fast walkway.

slides.label: the average fare for the moving sidewalk
slides.text: About an hour’s pay: Paris workers then earned 40 to 50 centimes an hour, and a ticket into the fair itself cost one franc.

slides.question: Which way did the exposition’s electric train run?
slides.explanation: It followed the walkway’s route in the opposite direction, sometimes 7 m up like the walkway, sometimes at ground level and sometimes underground.
